slides.title: How should a model and its tools share the work?
slides.notes:
RLM means recursive language model. It can delegate parts to helper models and use code.

Here we isolate a simpler building block: one model choosing actions and using tools. The game checks actual items, not persuasive text.

We test training examples and the division of work between model and code.

slides.title: Can examples teach a model how to choose its steps?
slides.notes:
We fine-tune Qwen3-4B using small LoRA adapters. A training row pairs the task, inventory and history with the next action.

Both teachers are programs; both show lookups. One uses known recipes to choose its route; the other discovers the route through lookups.

Same 32 tasks and 366 steps, but different histories and text lengths.

slides.title: The discovery examples led to more finished tasks.
slides.notes:
Each repeat means training both methods again with a different random seed. Each model makes 32 test attempts.

The chart shows 5 versus 15 and 3 versus 10. Task-group uncertainty intervals favor discovery in both repeats.

Changed recipes: 4 versus 6 and 1 versus 8, out of 16. The smaller difference remains uncertain.

slides.title: Code can handle details without choosing the plan.
slides.notes:
Code uses a recipe already in the public history. It preserves the chosen item and amount; it does not pick subgoals or reveal hidden recipes.

Four comparisons: 6 to 12, 8 to 10, 9 to 14, 9 to 13. Paired wins: 6/2/5/4; no losses.

Shared goals and generator, not 64 independent tasks. The smallest gain remains uncertain.

slides.title: The promising direction is learning and tools together.
slides.notes:
We have two promising effects, not a general solution to planning. Teaching packages differ in several ways; the mechanism is not isolated.

The queued test compares both teachers with and without code assistance on additional goals and recipe settings.

A second domain and later helper-call tests would strengthen the research.
